title: Shared state and races
sub: GetOrAdd, counters, Dictionary and the stop flag
cards/0/body:
Imagine a single notebook shared by everybody. While one person writes a number, another is already reading that line, and a third is erasing the line next to it. The result is a mess. That is a data race: the outcome depends on who got there first.

The loader has four shared "notebooks": the task map _loading, the finished-tile map _loaded, the counter _pending and the flag _stopRequested. Each one is handled carelessly.

For example, a Dictionary is safe if it is only read. But reading while another thread writes is not allowed: you can get garbage or an exception.
cards/1/title: GetOrAdd: "one value" does not mean "one factory call"
cards/1/body:
ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd(key, factory) guarantees that the dictionary ends up with one value for the key. But the factory is not under a lock. If two threads both miss the key at the same time, both call the factory. One result wins and the other is simply thrown away.

For a harmless factory ("create an object") that is fine. But our factory calls LoadAsync, which has already started: it took a semaphore spot, incremented _pending and went to the network. The discarded Task is not cancelled; it keeps running. The tile is downloaded twice.
cards/2/q: What is true about ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd(key, valueFactory)?
cards/2/options/0: There will be one value for the key, but valueFactory may run on several threads
cards/2/options/1: valueFactory runs under a lock, exactly once per key
cards/2/options/3: If the factory is slow, the dictionary blocks for all keys
cards/2/explain: The documentation says it: the factory runs outside the dictionary's internal locks, so it can run in parallel, and only one value is stored. The other results are discarded.
cards/2/wrong/1: That is exactly what GetOrAdd does not promise. If you need exactly one run, wrap the value in Lazy.
cards/3/body: Put a recipe in the dictionary instead of a running task: a Lazy<Task<Tile>>. You can create as many recipes as you like; they start nothing. The work starts on the first access to .Value, and by default Lazy guarantees the recipe runs once.
cards/3/deep: The default mode of Lazy<T> is ExecutionAndPublication: the factory runs once under a lock. But .Value starts LoadAsync right away on the caller's thread (until the first await), so the blocking Wait() from lesson 1 still has to go. And Lazy does not stop failures from being cached: an async method does not throw to the caller, the error goes into the Task, and Lazy keeps the failed task forever (more on that below).
cards/4/q: Complete GetTileAsync so that each tile is loaded exactly once.
cards/4/explain: Lazy delays the start of LoadAsync until .Value is read and makes sure it starts once. The Lazy wrapper that lost the GetOrAdd race is never unwrapped, so it starts nothing.
cards/5/task: Find four problems with state shared between threads. Tap the lines, then press Check.
cards/5/bugs/0/why: --_pending loses updates under a race, and the count can hit zero between two tiles: waiters think everything is loaded. A second SetResult throws InvalidOperationException.
cards/5/bugs/1/title: GetOrAdd with a side effect in the factory
cards/5/bugs/1/why: The factory can run on two threads at once: the tile loads twice and _pending and the semaphore are touched twice. Use Lazy<Task<Tile>>.
cards/5/bugs/2/title: Reading a Dictionary without a lock
cards/5/bugs/2/why: Other threads write to _loaded under a lock, but this code reads without one. Reading during a write gives garbage or an exception.
cards/5/bugs/3/why: Under the memory model, a plain bool shared across threads does not guarantee the loop will see the write: the JIT may read it once. Here the lock in Compact and the await save you by accident; a CancellationToken is the reliable way (volatile at the very least).
cards/6/title: The counter that hit zero at the wrong time
cards/6/body:
A scenario. Tiles A-D hold all four spots, _pending = 4, and tile E waits at the semaphore. A calls Release, E wakes up but has not reached Increment yet. Meanwhile A-D bring the counter down to 0 and announce: "everything is loaded!". The announcement came too early. Even simpler: the game requests tiles in waves, and the counter hits zero between waves.

When E finishes, the counter hits 0 again, and a second SetResult throws InvalidOperationException. That happens after Release: a tile that loaded fine returns an error, and the failed task stays in the cache. The fix: count at the point where work appears (in GetTileAsync), use Interlocked, and complete with TrySetResult.
cards/6/deep: One more subtlety: a TaskCompletionSource created without TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously runs the waiters' continuations synchronously inside SetResult. So foreign code after await WhenAllLoaded() starts running on the loading thread, inside our LoadAsync, and in general under whatever locks the caller of SetResult holds. That is why a TCS is almost always created with this flag.
cards/7/q: Put in order the events that make the counter hit zero too early.
cards/7/items/0: Tiles A-D hold all 4 spots, _pending = 4, tile E waits at the semaphore
cards/7/items/1: A calls Release, E wakes up but has not run Increment yet
cards/7/items/2: A-D bring the counter to 0, SetResult(true): "all done"
cards/7/items/3: E increments the counter, loads, brings it back to 0, and the second SetResult throws
cards/7/explain: The counter only counts loads that passed the semaphore, not loads that were already requested. So zero is possible while work still remains.
cards/8/q: Which fix for _pending and _allLoaded is the most reliable?
cards/8/options/0: Interlocked.Increment when a tile is queued, Interlocked.Decrement in finally, complete with TrySetResult
cards/8/options/3: Wrap SetResult in try/catch and swallow the exception
cards/8/explain: You need three things together: count at the right moment (when work appears), do it atomically, and survive a repeated completion.
cards/8/wrong/1: That is the same non-atomic code in different words.
cards/8/wrong/2: volatile gives visibility, not atomicity: --_pending is still a read, a subtract and a write.
cards/9/title: A failed task stays in the dictionary
cards/9/body:
While a Task sits in _loading, every later GetTileAsync(id) receives that same Task. If it ended with an error (or was cancelled), it stays that way. The network drops for one second and the tile is now "broken" until restart: nobody retries.

Failed entries must be removed. Cache success, not failure.
cards/9/deep: A subtlety: if the error happens synchronously, before GetOrAdd returns and the entry is in the dictionary, TryRemove does nothing, and the entry is added afterwards anyway. It is safer to remove in a continuation outside, once the task is already in the dictionary. Remove this exact task, not "whatever is under the key", or you may throw out a newer, successful attempt (in .NET 5+ use TryRemove(KeyValuePair); before that, ICollection<KeyValuePair>.Remove). Be careful with cancellation too: a task cancelled by someone else's token must not stay in the cache forever either.
cards/10/q: The tile server answered 503 for tile 42, then recovered. The player requests tile 42 again. What does the original loader return?
cards/10/options/0: The same failed Task: the error was cached
cards/10/explain: The dictionary stores a Task per key and never replaces it. Later calls get the same failed task until the entry is removed.
cards/11/q: Which of these is a data race in the loader?
cards/11/options/0: Reading _loaded.Count in the timer while another thread writes under a lock
cards/11/options/1: Two threads calling GetOrAdd for different keys at the same time
cards/11/options/2: A bool _stopRequested written on one thread and read in another thread's loop
cards/11/options/3: Reading the id variable inside the factory lambda
cards/11/explain: The first and the third: shared data, one thread writes, the other has no synchronization. ConcurrentDictionary is designed to be thread-safe for different keys, and id is a local, immutable parameter.
